item.title: Pro-life CEO predicts Trump FDA nominee could bring renewed scrutiny to abortion drug risks
item.description: Trump's FDA nominee Heidi Overton could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, says Americans United for Life CEO who calls her a "pro-life" pick.
item.content:encoded:
The chief executive of America's oldest pro-life organization told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's FDA nominee, Dr. Heidi Overton, could bring renewed scrutiny to mifepristone, the abortion drug at the center of an ongoing federal safety review.

John Mize, CEO of Americans United for Life (AUL), said he has had five or six conversations with Overton, who is known for her pro-life views. She currently serves as Trump's deputy assistant for domestic policy.

"I think she's going to bring objectivity to the issue of mifepristone in a way that will expose this drug for the damage it causes women," Mize said in an interview on Friday, adding that his organization is "optimistic" that Overton will be a "pro-life FDA commissioner."

Overton's nomination comes just weeks after an 18-year-old woman in North Carolina was accused of using mifepristone and misoprostol to terminate a pregnancy at 31 weeks, well beyond mifepristone's FDA-approved limit of 10 weeks.

HAWLEY INTRODUCES BILL TO STRIP FDA APPROVAL FROM 'INHERENTLY DANGEROUS' ABORTION PILL

Mize has led AUL for two-and-a-half years. The nonprofit has advocated against abortion, euthanasia, assisted suicide and other practices it considers threats to human life since its founding in 1971.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Mize said he believes Overton is the "right candidate" to lead the FDA, citing her experience in government, clinical medicine and medical research. If confirmed, Overton would take the reins of the agency responsible for regulating abortion medication, including mifepristone.

Mifepristone carries an FDA boxed warning, the agency’s strongest safety warning, for the risk of serious and sometimes fatal infections or bleeding.

Prompted initially by COVID-19 pandemic restrictions, the FDA stopped enforcing the drug's in-person dispensing requirement in 2021 and later removed it permanently after reviewing the available safety data.

Under current FDA rules, patients do not necessarily have to see a physician in person before receiving a prescription, allowing mifepristone to be prescribed after telehealth visit and mailed by a certified pharmacy. Mize wants those rules tightened.

SUPREME COURT TEMPORARILY BLOCKS APPEALS COURT RULING ON ABORTION PILL, RESTORES WIDER ACCESS TO DRUG

"Dr. Overton and I share a very similar perspective that the drug is dangerous, particularly in an unregulated way for women," Mize told Fox News Digital. "I firmly believe she understands the clinical implications of taking a drug with a black box warning and now shipping it in the mail."

Overton has publicly criticized mifepristone and other abortion drugs, which accounted for about 65% of clinician-provided abortions in 2023, according to the Guttmacher Institute, up from 53% in 2020 before the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade.

In a February 2023 policy brief for the America First Policy Institute, a MAGA-aligned think tank where she previously served as chief policy officer, Overton denounced federal policymakers for expanding access to abortion pills.

She also accused the Biden administration of using the COVID-19 pandemic to wrongly justify allowing mifepristone and misoprostol, a drug that induces early labor, to be sent to patients through the mail.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Taken together, the two drugs terminate early pregnancies: mifepristone blocks progesterone, a hormone needed to sustain the pregnancy, while misoprostol causes contractions that expel the fetus.

"Abortion is corrosive to children, women, and society broadly because it devalues and extinguishes innocent human life," she wrote at the time. "America First policies should focus on immediately halting the effort to normalize abortion-on-demand and on broadly recognizing the evidence of the risk posed to women."

Mize pointed to a 2025 study by the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank, that analyzed insurance claims from 865,727 mifepristone abortions between 2017 and 2023 and found a serious adverse event rate of nearly 11%. This included conditions such as hemorrhaging, sepsis or infection.

The study received immediate pushback, with the medical community saying it used a flawed methodology. The paper was also not peer-reviewed or published in a medical journal, factors Mize said Overton is aware of.

HAWLEY SENDS CRIMINAL REFERRAL OF 'LEFT-WING DARK-MONEY' GROUP OVER MAILED ABORTION DRUGS

"It's not the whole picture, and Dr. Overton would say that," Mize said. "But it's an important indicator as to what's happening in the real world. So I believe she will do a really good job of evaluating the study."

Mize said he hopes Overton will impose tighter restrictions on mifepristone after reviewing the evidence, potentially restoring a requirement that women see a doctor in person before receiving a prescription.

He described Overton as "measured" and "methodical" while cautioning that pro-life advocates should not expect her to pursue immediate, sweeping changes at the FDA.

"I don't get the sense that she's gonna move quickly on issues," Mize said.

SUPREME COURT KEEPS BROADER ACCESS TO ABORTION PILL MIFEPRISTONE IN PLACE WHILE LEGAL FIGHT CONTINUES

Dr. Marty Makary, the previous FDA commissioner, resigned in May after clashing with Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers. He also drew criticism from pro-life activists, who accused the agency under his leadership of slow-walking its safety review of mifepristone.

If confirmed, Overton would inherit the review, which was formally announced in September 2025 and does not have a scheduled completion date. The FDA has noted these types of studies typically take a year or longer to conduct.

After that review is completed, Mize said the next step for Overton, ideally, would be "a longer term, deep dive evaluation on this medication to determine if it should even be on the market."

Mize acknowledged that not all the evidence is in yet but made clear that his preference would be to take mifepristone off the market.

"From my perspective, any medication that denies someone the opportunity to live and kills a human being shouldn't be something that we're promoting amongst the FDA," Mize said. "Ultimately, I would love to see this drug removed from the market for those reasons. Culturally, we might not be there right now."

Overton’s confirmation hearing has not yet been scheduled but is expected to take place after the Senate returns from its summer recess on Sept. 14.

item.title: Jennifer Garner says she 'panicked' about financial stability after divorce from Ben Affleck
item.description: Jennifer Garner reveals she "panicked" about finances after her split from Ben Affleck, realizing she needed to become a serious earner for her kids.
item.content:encoded:
Jennifer Garner once "panicked" about her financial stability shortly after her marriage to Ben Affleck came to an end.

During an episode of the "Aspire with Emma Grede" podcast, Garner — who shares three children with Affleck — opened up about her past fear that she would no longer be able to financially support herself and her children post-divorce and explained how she pushed through. 

"I panicked when I was first out of my marriage and realized I had taken such a step back in my work," said Garner. "Suddenly I realized I don't know how long I'll be able to work. This isn't a career that's like, 'Hey, you're 60, you're 55, you're 43, come on, let's pay you more than you've ever made.' You know what I mean? That's not been traditionally the role. I was suddenly like, 'Wait a minute, I have to take care of myself, I have to take care of these kids. So what is it going to be?'"

JENNIE GARTH ADMITS ‘SCARY’ FINANCIAL SPIRAL AFTER ‘90210’ FAME

Garner said this was the time in her life where she couldn't pick up and leave for months at a time for a movie shoot. She had to be in Los Angeles for her children.

"I can't leave these kids for six months at a time," she said. "I would love to. I love going on location, but it's not this time in my career."

‘THE OFFICE’ STAR JENNA FISCHER EXPOSES THE GRUELING REALITY THAT FORCED HER OFF TV

Affleck and Garner met on the set of 2001's "Pearl Harbor," but didn't spark a romantic relationship until 2004, after starring alongside one another in the 2003 film "Daredevil." They married in 2005, but eventually called it quits in 2015.

"I was so lucky to be able to luxuriate and working some and being home and being a mom a lot of time," Garner said. "I was really grateful for that opportunity. I got to kind of have the best of both worlds, so I can't really look back and complain about any of it … it is what it is."

"It's not like you can just unfamous yourself. Life is expensive, and you still have to figure out how you're going to live," she added. "Just because you're well known by people does not mean that there is some great living being provided for you, and it became very serious to me, very quickly as someone who has never given a lot of thought to money, like, 'Oh I need to be an earner here.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Two years after her divorce, Garner became a co-founder of the organic children's food company, Once Upon A Farm.

Earlier this year, the "Alias" actress opened up about the "upheaval" that consumed her and their three children amid her very public split from Affleck.

"When my kids were little, I worked so little, and then we had such an upheaval in our family, that I really hardly worked for a long time," she told the outlet.

While balancing her work and professional life, Garner said she learned there is beauty in imperfection.

"You have to raise yourself at the same time. And just be so radically kind to yourself about how imperfect it is," she said of trying to navigate life as a working mom of three. "And that it is just going to be imperfect. There’s no such thing as balance. There’s no such thing as doing it right. And when the big moments happen, you are okay, and that’s on you to know and understand so your child feels your okayness."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

While expressing that same sentiment, Garner further opened up about the sacrifices made while raising their three children together. 

"When your kids grow up in two separate households, I become mom and dad, and he becomes dad and mom," said Garner. "You kind of can't help it, right? Because you don't have the benefit of both sides, the yin and yang being in the same house, so you have to have a bit of both in the way you parent."

"There's a little bit of loss in that, but there's also something gained in that," she added. "You also just learn, it's made me let go and not focus so much on the bringing up."

item.title: CNN, MS NOW has mentioned Trump aide Natalie Harp hundreds of times since Ossoff's viral jab
item.description: Natalie Harp's name was mentioned over 700 times on CNN and MS NOW over the past several days after Jon Ossoff's viral stump speech sparked a firestorm.
item.content:encoded:
CNN and MS NOW have gone wall-to-wall covering one of President Donald Trump's most trusted aides.

Natalie Harp was dragged into a political firestorm after being name-dropped in a viral stump speech by Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who appeared to suggest that she and Trump had an inappropriate relationship — though Ossoff has attempted to distance himself from the innuendo.

Now more than one week removed from Ossoff's comment, the liberal news networks have gone into overdrive with their fixation on the 35-year-old White House staffer.

JON OSSOFF'S CONTROVERSIAL TRUMP JAB SPARKS MEDIA FEEDING FRENZY OVER WHITE HOUSE AIDE NATALIE HARP

Between last Monday through last Sunday, Harp's name was mentioned at least 308 times on CNN and a whopping 344 times on MS NOW within the seven-day period, according to Grabien transcripts.

That relentless coverage of Harp continued this week. CNN's mentions of Harp have ticked up to 318, while MS NOW has surpassed 400 mentions through mid-Tuesday.

Both networks gave breathless attention to reports of the letters Harp had written to Trump expressing staunch loyalty and how she was within Trump's tight-knit circle who joined him on his secret plane switch out of Turkey last month.

CNN FIRES BACK AT TRUMP WHITE HOUSE OVER ATTACKS ON REPORTER, CALLS THEM 'BENEATH THE OFFICE'

MS NOW reported how Harp doesn't have a security clearance despite her close access to the president, while CNN dug up old social media posts showing her "zealous" support for Trump on Jan. 6. 

CNN previously reported, citing unnamed sources, that Harp allegedly "jumped into an SUV trunk" to ride with Trump for an October 2023 court appearance because she "wouldn’t take no for an answer" when the vehicle didn't have enough room.

CNN also drew intense backlash among conservatives for interviewing Harp's estranged brother, Preston Harp, on air.

WHITE HOUSE TEARS INTO OSSOFF WITH BRUTAL TAKEDOWN AFTER JAB AT KEY TRUMP AIDE: ‘LIGHTWEIGHT LOSER’

Additionally, the White House sharply admonished CNN White House correspondent Kristen Holmes for asking Trump about Ossoff's comment, prompting CNN's fiery response in defense of its reporter, calling the attacks against her "beneath the office."

Curtis Houck, the managing editor of NewsBusters of the conservative watchdog Media Research Center, told Fox News Digital that CNN and MS NOW have "gone full bore" on Harp because of their vehement opposition to Trump.

"They're more than willing to invoke someone else and drag their name through the mud," Houck said. "And I think it's really sick and disgusting."

Representatives for CNN and MS NOW did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: DOJ sues to stop Ohio court blocking courthouse arrests
item.description: The Justice Department sued Franklin County Municipal Court over a rule blocking ICE civil arrests without a judicial warrant, citing federal law.
item.content:encoded:
The Justice Department sued an Ohio court Tuesday over a new rule blocking federal immigration arrests at or near the courthouse, accusing local officials of unlawfully interfering with federal enforcement and forcing ICE agents to make arrests in potentially riskier settings.

At issue is a Franklin County Municipal Court rule, which bars civil arrests at the courthouse unless officers have a judicial warrant. The DOJ argues the rule conflicts with federal immigration law, which allows ICE agents in certain circumstances to make arrests with administrative warrants or no warrant at all.

"This type of rule obstructs federal law enforcement and facilitates evasion of federal law by dangerous criminal aliens, despite Congress’s direction that federal agents detain and remove them," said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division. "Throughout the country, and including in this courthouse specifically, federal agents have routinely and safely conducted arrests. The Department of Justice is committed to protecting that important federal prerogative."

JUDGE BLOCKS PHILADELPHIA LAW TARGETING MASKED FEDERAL OFFICERS

Those arrests can be less predictable and more dangerous because they may take place at homes, workplaces or other public locations, according to the complaint.

Two Columbus ICE officers have been hospitalized after encountering violence during at-large arrests in the past three months, DOJ says. The complaint does not identify the officers or provide details about the incidents.

ICE has also had to conduct longer surveillance and field operations to find people away from the courthouse. DOJ says an arrest at a jail or courthouse may require two officers, while an arrest in the field typically requires four to six.

The department says courthouses offer a safer, more controlled setting because people entering are generally screened for weapons and other contraband. ICE agents have also coordinated with courthouse security and generally waited until hearings ended before making arrests, according to the complaint.

ICE made at least 12 arrests at Franklin County Municipal Court in recent years before the rule was adopted, DOJ says.

Rule 2.10 prohibits civil arrests of people at the courthouse for a proceeding or other lawful court business, but makes an exception for arrests carried out with a warrant issued by a judge.

item.title: Nick Hogan helps guide Hulkamania into future with sports bar outside MSG, shares thoughts on father's legacy
item.description: Nick Hogan reveals plans for Hulk Hogan's SLAM Sports Bar next to Madison Square Garden, calling it a throwback to when Hulkamania ruled NYC.
item.content:encoded:
Hulk Hogan may have died last July, but Hulkamania will certainly live forever.

In the heart of New York City, right outside of Madison Square Garden, Nick Hogan and his project partner Rich Rosen are preparing to write the next chapter of Hulkamania’s legacy with Hulk Hogan’s SLAM Sports Bar to help honor pro wrestling history and the legends that shaped the industry. The bar is set to open soon.

COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK

"The location is so special and it's right next door to Madison Square Garden, right at the entrance to the Garden and Penn Station," Nick Hogan told OutKick in a recent interview. "It's like a really central hub spot for New York City. So, we're thrilled to bring this concept to New York City, but also to the birthplace and the spiritual home of Hulkamania.

"So, with those renders being what they are, when this place comes to life and we're all lit up and it's grand opening week, there's going to be magic in the air. We're going to have so many of our friends and family there and the experience that the fans will get is going to be unique and unlike anything they'll be able to get anywhere else in the world. I mean just the connection alone to Hulkamania and the unique ability that we're going to have to give people that magic again is going to be amazing. So, we're thrilled about it."

Rosen, a lifelong New Yorker, said he’s been going to Madison Square Garden since the 1970s and has seen larger-than-life athletes come into the building – from Hulk Hogan and Bruno Sammartino to Muhammad Ali and Michael Jordan. He dreamt of bringing Hogan’s brand to New York City and making it his own and bringing in big-time players like ICRAVE to help design the bar.

He said he hoped Hulk Hogan’s SLAM Sports Bar will be a throwback to a simpler time for future patrons.

"What we're really hoping in Slam, besides all the future and incredible effects that ICRAVE is bringing into this — sound effects and lighting effects — what you really want is you want actually a throwback," Rosen explained. "You want people to be able to step back in time when Hulkamania took over New York City in the 1980s, and ‘90s, and when things were a lot more fun than they are now, so to speak. I think everybody could admit to that.

"Now, you're giving people a chance to go to Madison Square Garden and see the world champs play and then go across the street and go back in time. And as they watch the future games and the Super Bowls and the NBA championships, they'll also be able to reflect back in time when they enjoyed themselves and when New York was at the top of its peak. It really is going to be a gift to New York City above everything else. It's finally going to have a worthy spot next to Madison Square Garden with its most famous performer."

Nick Hogan has since carried the torch to honor and preserve his father’s legacy inside and outside the ring.

For him, Hulkamania is now something that bridges the gap between all generations of sports fans.

"It means everything to me, and like Rich just mentioned, is that this is spanning past, present, and future," Hogan said. "And it's like looking at his legacy in terms of what he left behind and all of the iconic moments that he had. It's almost like a point of reflection for me where my perspective has changed, and his legacy is not just the past, but it's the future as well. And it's what he inspires others to do and how he touched other people's lives. And what he's inspired us to do is to carry that legacy forward in a way that he could and his spirit could, and what the Hulkamania mantra is.

"So, that's what we're so thrilled about is, like Rich said, this bridges the gap between past, present, and future. As you're sitting in Slam Sports Bar in our main room, the Slam room, and you're reflecting, you're looking around, you see the old wrestling matches on TV, but right next to it, you see tonight's game. And then, you just might have left the concert at the Garden, and then you're getting thrilled to come back in a few days for the Knicks game or something. It gives people a place to go and reflect and take in all of those iconic moments and celebratory moments and also get excited for the ones that are coming in the future. So, that's a really cool concept for us to be able to do that. And also, that's kind of the spirit of the Hulkamania — that Hulkamania will live forever. And my dad always said that Hulkamania will outlive the man. He definitely wasn't wrong about that. So, it's extremely important to me to carry the legacy forward in the same way that he had intended and through Slam Sports Bar, we're able to do that."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS

Hulk Hogan was still beloved by many through his death last year.

Though he heard the boo birds in his last appearance on WWE TV, Nick Hogan made clear that his father is the "most important figure in professional wrestling entertainment."

"Truthfully, I think what matters the most is that I think that he single-handedly is the most important figure in professional wrestling entertainment, and bar none," he told OutKick. "I think that there's a lot of Mount Rushmore guys. There's a lot of guys that really are incredible that were fantastic at moving the needle and everything else, but I think that he above all else is by far the most responsible for bringing it to the masses and for giving it the wild popularity that it's got today.

"And there's a lot of other guys that can be credited for that as well. I just think that my dad moved the needle more than anyone else."

item.title: 'Not 1984': Flock cameras watching millions of Americans spark bipartisan revolt
item.description: Flock Safety's automatic license plate readers face bipartisan backlash as lawmakers warn AI-powered cameras threaten Fourth Amendment privacy rights.
item.content:encoded:
There's a new frontier in the national privacy debate that's uniting people on the right and left, and it's a tool that millions of Americans encounter every day without even realizing it.

Automatic license plate reader (ALPR) companies have been brought under scrutiny by lawmakers in Washington as privacy hawks warn that the growing sophistication of artificial intelligence (AI) technology is testing the bounds of what ALPR devices can legally learn about drivers on the road.

One company in particular, Flock Safety, has been taking hits in the media and political sphere as news of Flock cameras' misuse — and occasional success — dominates headlines.

"There's cameras everywhere, people know that, but if law enforcement has the ability to monitor the comings and goings of citizens, I think that's wrong. I mean, we're not the CCP, we're not 1984 and an Orwellian society, and Americans have rights," Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital.

LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

He pointed to a recent incident in his district where a now-former Sarasota police officer was fired and arrested after being accused of misusing Flock camera technology, using it to spy on one particular license plate over 300 times.

FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES

"I don't think you're gonna be able to stop these cameras from being out there, but at the very least, there should be some type of legal parameters put in place to protect people's Fourth Amendment rights," he said.

ALPRs automatically capture and analyze vehicle and location data on public roads without drivers' consent. Supporters have argued that it's a critical tool for public safety that only collects minimal information, while opponents labeled it an alarming expansion of the mass surveillance state.

LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS AT HOME DEPOT AND LOWE’S SPARK PRIVACY FEARS

Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital, "These cameras are well beyond an automated license plate reader today. AI has made them so capable that they are now capable of facial recognition, of seeing what you’re doing inside your car. So it’s well beyond the license plate reader…that’s the problem. Technology has moved these beyond just looking at the back of a car."

On the other side of the aisle, a spokesperson for progressive Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., pointed Fox News Digital to her recent comments responding to news that Flock was updating its oversight standards. Ramirez wrote on X, "Private tech companies have amassed record-breaking profits off our pain and the use of technology for mass surveillance is a threat to our democracy, civil liberties, and privacy. Congress must stop the ever-expanding surveillance state."

‘DARTH VADER’ USES DARK SIDE TO MOCK CONTROVERSIAL SURVEILLANCE CAMERAS: 'THE EMPEROR IS A FAN OF FLOCK'

The debate even exploded onto the campaign trail ahead of November's midterm elections, where ALPRs join AI data centers as Big Tech's big boogeymen.

"I oppose Flock’s mass surveillance technology, and I’ll stand with anyone in Congress, regardless of party, who wants to put limits on unchecked mass surveillance on the American people," Will Lawrence, a Democrat running for the House in Michigan's 7th Congressional District, told Fox News Digital.

DSA CANDIDATE PUSHES FEDERAL AI DATA CENTER MORATORIUM WITH MICHIGAN EARLY VOTING UNDERWAY

Abdul El-Sayed, the insurgent progressive Democratic nominee for Senate in Michigan, accused his opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers, R-Mich., of supporting Flock cameras in a campaign video released on X.

"There's been this mass proliferation of black cameras, any and everywhere, little cameras, watching your every move to collect information about you without you even noticing," he said in the video. "If you believe, like me, that you shouldn't just be surveilled because you're driving along the street, then I hope I can earn your support."

A spokesperson for Rogers told Fox News Digital that he "vehemently opposes unchecked use of Flock cameras to track law-abiding citizens. Security and liberty aren’t enemies. Good government protects both."

Back on Capitol Hill, the furor over these cameras has prompted a flurry of legislative pushback.

Self is among the House lawmakers pushing bills aimed at the issue, along with Reps. Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

Steube told Fox News Digital that he's also "looking at filing something at the national level," and is sending a letter to Sarasota, Florida, officials threatening to withhold federal funding absent a promise of "reasonable restrictions" to "prevent the abuses that have happened right here in our backyard."

Privacy and misuse concerns have sparked efforts across the country to cut ties with Flock specifically, from Lansing, Michigan, to Bernadillo County, New Mexico.

Flock is just one company of several that operate ALPRs, some of which have been used for years.

But the technology does have its benefits and has been used to stop crime.

Flock Safety founder and CEO Garrett Langley told Fox News' "Saturday in America" that his technology has helped police find missing children at least twice, including after a recent carjacking in Atlanta. Flock has also said it does not use facial recognition and recently introduced new safety controls in response to the public backlash.

"When I think about legislation that calls for an outright ban, that's like banning vehicles. That would never have made sense. Instead, what we did is we introduced laws against drunk driving. We introduced laws around seatbelts, laws around airbags," Langley said. "What happens if law enforcement abuses this powerful technology today? It is too often that in Flock and in other technologies, there's no regulation, there's no accountability. And we think that's wrong."

Supporters of ALPRs like Flock cameras have held them up as a key crime-fighting tool, while agreeing that guardrails to prevent abuse would be helpful.

"I think it's definitely a net positive. And I think that's a very easy call... the use cases and the documented cases of these things being effective tools, I think, vastly outnumber the handful of cases of abuse and misuse that we've seen," Rafael Mangual, a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, told Fox News Digital. "The fact that some police officers will misuse their firearms, for example, to hurt people, is not a reason to take away all police officers' firearms."

Mangual said he disagreed with accusations of Fourth Amendment violations as well: "I think as of right now, these cameras can't be used to do the sorts of things that courts have recognized require a warrant."

Jim Pasco, executive director of the National Fraternal Order of Police, told Fox News Digital, "There’s an awful lot of new and still developing technology out there that's very helpful to law enforcement and to enhancing public safety. That said, all of these systems need to be regulated to ensure that they aren't abused."

He also cautioned against making policy decisions in the heat of an election cycle.

"The most dangerous time of governance to have a crisis in is an even-numbered year, because elections are always held in even-numbered years. And I would say this problem and this year are no exception," Pasco said. "There needs to be a very careful analysis of the benefits and the risks inherent in abuse and any action that's taken should, if anything, enhance the potential for these systems being used for good and minimize the chances of abuse."

"Let's not throw out the baby with the bath water here."

item.title: 'Serial defecator' on the loose in Tulsa, last seen wearing a thong, mask with a hole cut out & a shower cap

REPEATEDLY FLASHING OTHERS AT A PARK IS HOW YOU TURN UNDERWEAR HIKES INTO AN INDECENT EXPOSURE ARREST

item.title: Jury convicts Kevin Salazar in execution-style killing of LA Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer
item.description: Kevin Salazar was convicted of murdering Los Angeles County Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer in a 2023 drive-by ambush near his Palmdale station.
item.content:encoded:
A California man has been convicted in the drive-by ambush of a Los Angeles deputy shot and killed at a red light just steps from the sheriff's Palmdale station in 2023.

Jurors found Kevin Salazar, 32, guilty of the murder of Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer Monday after a week-long trial.

"It’s very helpful that the justice system prevail, that you have a conviction that is a benefit to the family," Brad Gage, the Los Angeles attorney representing Clinkunbroomer's family, told Fox News Digital. "That gives some solace. That gives some comfort."

MURDERED LOS ANGELES SHERIFF'S DEPUTY'S FAMILY SLAPS COUNTY WITH $20M WRONGFUL DEATH LAWSUIT

Around 6 p.m. on Sept. 16, 2023, Clinkunbroomer pulled up to a red light down the street from the sheriff's station in Palmdale. He was driving his marked car and wearing his uniform. As he waited for the light to turn green, another car pulled up alongside him – and a man inside shot him in the head.

Authorities said Salazar had followed Clinkunbroomer from the Palmdale Sheriff's Station to the intersection less than a block away before opening fire with a .22 revolver. He sped off, and Clinkunbroomer was pronounced dead at a hospital.

Authorities found Salazar at his family's home in Palmdale two days later and arrested him on murder charges after a standoff, part of which was caught on video.

ARREST MADE IN AMBUSH KILLING OF LA SHERIFF'S DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

Clinkunbroomer, 30, was engaged to be married at the time of his murder.

"When a parent loses a child, there’s no name for it," Gage said. "It’s so painful, it’s so traumatic, it is so devastating that it is beyond words."

Jurors deliberated for just 2 1/2 hours before finding Salazar guilty of first-degree murder as well as the special circumstance allegations of murder of a peace officer, lying in wait and firing from a vehicle, according to the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.

Despite the conviction, a motive remains unclear, according to the family's attorney.

"As far as we know, there was no reason," Gage told Fox News Digital. "It was just execution of a police officer."

The court will move on Wednesday to a sanity-deciding phase for Salazar, to determine whether he goes to prison or is confined in a state mental hospital after he raised an insanity defense.

SEND US A TIP

"This brutal and senseless murder took the life of a dedicated deputy, leaving his family, colleagues and community to endure an unimaginable loss. We hope today’s guilty verdict brings a measure of healing to Deputy Clinkunbroomer’s family and loved ones," Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement.

Clinkunbroomer came from a law enforcement family. His grandfather, father and brother all served.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Ryan dedicated his life to service, proudly carrying on his family’s legacy as a third-generation member of the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department," Sheriff Robert Luna said after the verdict. "We will forever honor his service, his sacrifice and the badge he proudly wore. Deputy Ryan Clinkunbroomer will never be forgotten."

After his death, the family sued the county, alleging that mandatory overtime and understaffing had left Clinkunbroomer exhausted and more vulnerable to the ambush, Gage said.

The county was dismissed from the lawsuit based on workers' compensation protections, however, and the family decided not to pursue a civil case against Salazar.

Separately, the county honored Clinkunbroomer by renaming a Department of Parks and Recreation sports complex after him in January 2026.

item.title: James Carville goes nuclear on Jeffries over Jared Kushner sit-down and demands Democrats draw a line
item.description: James Carville slammed Hakeem Jeffries for meeting with Jared Kushner, saying Democrats universally agree they don't sit down with Donald Trump's inner circle.
item.content:encoded:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville tore into House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., on Monday over his meeting with U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner, saying Democrats of every viewpoint agree on one thing: they don't sit down with President Donald Trump's inner circle.

The takedown came just days after news broke that Jeffries had sat down with Trump’s son-in-law to discuss housing, immigration and high living costs as possible categories of common ground, The New York Times first reported.

"Let me try to explain something," Carville said. "And Hakeem, you’re a smart guy. Let me explain something here, very, very clear. You have Democrats that have a different position on Medicare for all, whether that’s a good idea. You have Democrats that have different positions on effective policing, and there’s a whole variety of subjects of which there are some disagreements within the Democratic Party."

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

Despite the seemingly good-faith meeting, Carville told Jeffries that Democrats’ ability to find compromise does not extend across party lines.

"On one thing, on one thing, there is no disagreement," he said. "There’s unanimity. And it is simply this: in the opinion of every Democrat in the United States, progressive, moderate, middle road, left, f---, I don’t know whatever you want, we believe one thing above all."

CARVILLE UNLOADS ON DSA SOCIALISTS: 'DON'T USE OUR GOD---- NAME'

"These people are a pack of felons and traitors, and you do not meet with them. You do not meet with them," Carville continued.

Carville went on to offer his own suggestion for what he believes the best course of action would be for Democrats looking to see eye-to-eye with Kushner.

"We need to drag [Kushner’s] a-- before a committee and find out what backdoor-dealing, w----house s--- he's got going on with Steve Whitcomb and everybody else," Carville said. "We're not going to be nice to you. We don't like you."

Carville also added that Trump and his administration "have no idea what they’re doing," while accusing them of "making every backdoor bulls--- deal they can."

CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS MAY NEED TO BLOCK FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES FROM JOINING CAUCUS, MODERATE GROUP DISAGREES

CARVILLE TORCHES DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS AS 'PACK OF FOOLS,' PRAISES AOC'S POLITICAL EVOLUTION

The veteran strategist ended with a single line of advice to Jeffries: "And we don’t meet with them. Don’t meet with them."

In light of the fallout following Jeffries’ meeting with Kushner, Axia CEO Jason Mudd told Fox News Digital the biggest problem Jeffries is facing is the fact that the news of the meeting came out after it had been held.

JEFFRIES' SOCIALISM DILEMMA: NEW YORK VICTORIES EXPOSE DEMOCRATIC PARTY DIVIDE

"Jeffries got caught being reasonable in private without being strategic in public. To be clear, this isn't about whether Kushner deserved the meeting. It's about how the meeting was handled," Mudd said. "Now Jeffries is explaining it after the leak instead of framing it before the leak. That's the real mistake. Not taking the meeting itself."

Mudd went on to acknowledge that politicians often do have to compromise with members of opposing parties, but should do so while remaining transparent with their constituents.

The public relations CEO and expert added that to mitigate the fallout, he would suggest Jeffries provide full insight into his meeting with Kushner as a way to regain trust within his party.

"If I were advising Jeffries or his camp right now, I'd tell him to stop playing defense and take control of the narrative today," Mudd said. "Say what the meeting was about, why he took it, and what came of it, in his own words. Silence and vague statements read as guilt even when there's nothing to hide, and right now the story is being written for him and without him."

Fox News Digital reached out to Jeffries, Kushner and the White House for comment.

item.title: Dem House hopeful defended music video showing woman restrained, groped and killed
item.description: Bobby Pulido defended Gerardo Ortiz's graphic music video depicting sexual violence, adding to controversies as he challenges Monica De La Cruz.
item.content:encoded:
In a 2016 interview, Latin Grammy Award-winning artist and Democratic congressional candidate Bobby Pulido defended a fellow singer against criticism for a graphic music video that depicted acts of sexual violence and murder.

In the video production of "Fuiste Mía" or "You were mine" by Gerardo Ortiz, a singer walks in on his girlfriend cheating on him. After shooting her lover, he then handcuffs her to a pole, blindfolds her, and gropes her before putting her in the trunk of his car and setting it on fire.

In response to backlash, Pulido defended Ortiz, calling the video a matter of artistic direction.

"I've made videos with suggestive images; some have stayed, others have been edited, and still others were never used. That's the decision of the artist and their team," Pulido said in response to public backlash against the production.

Pulido’s resurfaced response to the music video is the latest in a series of controversies he has tried to downplay as he pursues a seat in the U.S. House of Representatives in Texas’ 15th Congressional District — one of the country’s most competitive seats.

FORMER DISNEY TEEN STAR EXPOSES CHILLING WARNING SIGNS OF PREDATORY BEHAVIOR IN HOLLYWOOD

Pulido is best known for Tejano, or Mexican–Spanish folk-style, songs like "Desvelado" and "Se Murió de Amor," and received five nominations for a Latin Grammy Awards, winning Best Tejano Album in 2025 and 2022.

He filed to run for Congress in Texas’ 15th District, challenging Rep. Monica De La Cruz, R-Texas. A two-term incumbent, she last won election to the district in 2024 in a 57.1% to 42.9% victory over Democratic nominee Michelle Vallejo. 

Along the way, Pulido has drawn scrutiny for a resurfaced history of posting links to explicit websites on his personal X account — as well as for a social media post of what appeared to be him urinating on President Donald Trump’s Hollywood Walk of Fame star. Pulido has shrugged off criticism for both, stating in 2024 that it's "it’s impossible to have Twitter and not watch porn," and that he had only poured water on Trump’s star as a joke.

More notably, Pulido has also had to fend off criticisms of bringing a registered sex offender to a Texas middle school benefit concert in 2018.

DEM TIED TO CARTEL OPERATIVE SAYS 'WHITE NATIONALISTS' JOINING IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT TO 'HUNT DOWN PEOPLE'

In that case, Pulido denied knowledge of his associate’s status at the time and has dismissed coverage of it as a "nothing story," according to Axios.

Similarly, in his defense of Ortiz, Pulido downplayed the music video, arguing that viewers had become accustomed to increasingly graphic images.

"What happens when there's a [car] accident?" Pulido asked, comparing the music video to real-life instances of tragedy.

"Traffic doesn't flow because people slow down or even stop to see what happened; something similar happens with the regional Mexican genre when these kinds of incidents occur."

At least one Republican onlooker is left unconvinced by the defense of the music video — and defenses of other past behaviors.

"Bobby Pulido has spent his entire adult life defending perverts and predators while lashing out at members of law enforcement who keep Texans safe. He is a truly sick individual who is morally rotten," Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee (RNC), said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

DEM RIPPED FOR ‘DISGUSTING’ ABSENCE ON BILL TO PUNISH VIOLENT CRIMINALS AFTER GIRL STRANGLED IN GRISLY KILLING

The Pulido campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment about his defense of the video and whether he had a track record of downplaying potentially problematic conduct.

item.title: Muslim Brotherhood-linked networks embedded across Canadian institutions, new report alleges

TURKEY’S NATO ROLE UNDER SCRUTINY AMID NEW REPORT ON HAMAS, MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD TIES

item.title: Keep an eye on these under-the-radar names during this season's college football coaching carousel
item.description: Florida State, South Carolina, and Baylor all face hot seat questions as the 2026 college football coaching carousel predictions take shape.
item.content:encoded:
Every year in the modern era of college football, dozens of head coaches go into the season on what we like to call a "hot seat."

This means there's a very good chance that they don't make it through the end of the season, and 2026 is no exception.

After witnessing an absolutely historic coaching carousel in 2025 that saw job openings at perennial powerhouse programs like LSU, Florida, and Penn State, the expectation is that this year's carousel will take a step back.

RANKING THE TEN BEST COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHES IN THE COUNTRY AHEAD OF THE 2026 SEASON

However, that doesn't mean we won't see plenty of premiere programs in the market for head coaches by the end of the season, as teams like Florida State, South Carolina, and Baylor all have coaches with exceedingly hot seats heading into the fall.

The question is: who will replace those head coaches once they're given the boot?

A lot of marquee names from the last hiring cycle are just now settling into their new digs, so some of these once-proud programs might have to find their next captain to steer the ship from some unlikely places.

Here are a few names that you might not know just yet, but could be coaching at big-time programs in 2027.

When you think of stable, winning college football programs, your mind probably doesn't immediately go to the UTSA Roadrunners, but that is precisely what head coach Jeff Traylor has turned them into.

He guided the Roadrunners to two of the best seasons in program history in 2021 and 2022, which included their first appearance in the AP Poll and first conference championship, and has three straight bowl victories to boot.

'HOT SEAT RANKINGS' FOR ALL 16 SEC COACHES AS BEGINNING OF 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON DRAWS NEARER

Aside from a two-year stint as Arkansas' running backs coach, Traylor has spent his entire career in the Lone Star State, and that is significant for the sole fact that a job could be opening up just three hours north on I-35.

I mentioned Baylor having a coach on the hot seat, and if the Bears decide to pull the trigger and fire Dave Aranda, I believe Traylor should be one of their first calls.

He has deep ties to the state of Texas and even coached high school football for a decade and a half at powerhouse Gilmer, which could help a ton with recruiting in-state talent.

It feels like Traylor is ready for a step up to the big-leagues of Power 4 football, and Baylor seems like the logical choice to make that transition as comfortable as possible.

Staying in the Lone Star State, the Houston Cougars are coming off a brilliant 2025 campaign in which they won ten games and finished in the top-25 of the AP Poll, and the man they have to thank for that is head coach Willie Fritz.

If you aren't familiar with Fritz, you certainly remember his former team, the Tulane Green Wave, upsetting Lincoln Riley's USC Trojans in the Cotton Bowl back in 2022.

That's right, before Jon Sumrall was leading Tulane to the College Football Playoff, Fritz had them busting down the doors of a New Year's Six Bowl.

item.title: Air Force officer who died in Alaska plane crash remembered as 'positive leader'
item.description: The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah Borsich, 23, as a victim of the deadly Alaska charter plane crash that killed all eight on board near Cape Newenham.
item.content:encoded:
A 23-year-old Air Force officer killed alongside seven others in a charter plane crash in remote western Alaska last week is being remembered as a "positive leader" who served with "professionalism, compassion and purpose."

The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 450 miles west-southwest of Anchorage. Borsich was a project programmer with the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson.

"Lt. Borsich was a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command," Col. Timothy Meerstein, commander of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, said in a statement.

TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH

"She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her," Meerstein said. "She made a lasting impact on our team, and we are grateful for her service and commitment to our nation."

The Cessna 441 was carrying two pilots and six passengers when it crashed west of Cape Newenham at about 12:15 p.m. Thursday. All eight people aboard were killed.

The charter plane had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and was headed to Cape Newenham when it crashed during its second approach to the gravel runway in heavy fog, according to federal officials.

The pilots could not see the runway and were flying by instruments, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said Friday. They aborted their first landing attempt because of poor visibility before crashing on the second approach.

An observation system near the airport reported fog and visibility of about 10 miles shortly before the crash. About 15 minutes later, visibility had fallen to less than a quarter-mile, according to the National Weather Service.

Search teams later found fragmented wreckage from the twin-engine plane, also known as a Cessna Conquest.

The Air Force said an Army member, contractors and crew members with Anchorage-based airplane charter company Security Aviation were also among those killed.

"We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten."

Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash.

"Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy."

Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause.

"Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said.

In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas.

ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE

The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform.

Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China.

Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said.

Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment."

"This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash.

The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the crash.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: PGA Tour is finally bringing match play to its postseason beginning in 2028 in no-brainer decision
item.description: The PGA Tour Championship will feature a 32-player, two-week match play format starting in 2028, replacing the current FedEx Cup finale structure.
item.content:encoded:
Finally, after years of begging from golf fans, the PGA Tour is introducing match play to its postseason beginning in 2028.

In June, the Tour announced that it will roll out an entirely new competitive structure starting in 2028 with two different tracks, the PGA Tour Championship Series and the PGA Tour Challenger Series. It was assumed that the finale for the Championship Series would include some form of match play, and the Tour made it official with an announcement laying out all of the details on Tuesday.

The Top 90 finishers on the PGA Tour Championship Series points list will retain their membership cards for the following year, and those 90 players will also qualify for the Championship Series Finale. The 90-player, 72-hole stroke play event will essentially serve as the first playoff event, which will then lead into a match play event that will take place across two weeks.

RORY MCILROY GETS SNARKY ON THE RETURN OF LIV GOLF PLAYERS TO PGA TOUR: 'HAVE THEY BROUGHT VALUE?'

The Championship Series Finale will award two separate titles - the season-long points winner and winner of the stroke play event - and the Top 32 players on the final season-long points list will advance to match play.

The two-week event will still be called the Tour Championship, but it will be the first of its kind.

The first week will see the 32-player field split into eight groups of four that will compete in group match play across three days. The top two players in each group will then advance to the second week of the Tour Championship.

In a fun wrinkle worth mentioning, if there is a tie at the conclusion of group play, a playoff will take place to determine who will advance, instead of any sort of margin-of-victory tiebreaker or any others determined on paper.

The second week of match play will feature 16 players who will compete in match play across four days, with the last man standing being the player who manages to win four consecutive matches.

The second week of the Tour Championship will be held at a different venue than the first week of the event. The PGA Tour stated that a full lineup of dates and venues for the 2028 Championship Series will be unveiled on February 22, 2027.

Since the FedEx Cup was first introduced in 2007, serving as the PGA Tour's postseason, the Tour has rolled out multiple formats. From a straightforward season-long points race to giving the points leader a cushion on the leaderboard, and now the simple format of awarding the FedEx Cup to the winner of the Tour Championship, the postseason has long needed a boost.

Making the season finale a match play event – which most would agree is not only the most entertaining but also the best format to determine a champion – was the easiest change to make. PGA Tour commissioner Jay Monahan never got around to making it. Soon-to-be PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp announcing the change before he officially assumes his new role on January 1, 2027, can certainly be seen as a surprising sign of what's to come for the Tour and its fans.

The PGA Tour axed its WGC-Match Play event held in Austin, Texas, following the 2023 tournament. While the match play event typically fell at an odd time on the calendar, it was beloved by the overwhelming majority of fans as it was something different.

Having a two-week match play event to close out the year on two separate courses should provide nothing but positive returns for all involved.

item.title: 9/11 victim's identity emerges nearly 25 years later after DNA breakthrough cracks mystery
item.description: A first-of-its-kind forensic genealogy technique helped New York City investigators identify a World Trade Center victim nearly 25 years after 9/11.
item.content:encoded:
Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a family has finally received an answer after New York City investigators used a first-of-its-kind DNA and genealogy technique to identify a woman killed at the World Trade Center.

The adult woman, whose name is being withheld at her family’s request, is the first World Trade Center victim identified through forensic investigative genetic genealogy, New York City officials announced Sunday.

Her identification marks the 1,654th person identified from remains recovered after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 2,753 people in New York City.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

The breakthrough came through a collaboration between the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and the NYPD’s Investigative Genetic Genealogy Squad. The technique pairs specialized DNA analysis with genealogy research to generate leads that are then confirmed through forensic testing.

"As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific September 11 attacks, we honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "We remain committed to the families who have spent 25 years waiting for answers."

REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY

Forensic investigative genetic genealogy has emerged as a powerful tool in cold cases, allowing investigators to trace family connections from DNA evidence and identify people who may otherwise have remained unknown.

Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Jason Graham said the new method could help advance the city’s long-running effort to identify those killed in the attacks.

WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT

"This sacred commitment is propelled by our dedication to apply the most innovative scientific techniques," Graham said. "FIGG represents a promising new addition to our toolkit."

Officials said they are also using renewed family outreach and continued DNA retesting to link recovered remains to victims already identified.

But the work remains unfinished. About 1,099 World Trade Center victims, roughly 40% of those killed, have yet to be identified.

The woman is the first newly identified World Trade Center victim since August 2025, officials said.
